title: Org audit pipeline requires flush(), not commit()
description: The OrgOps audit subsystem uses post-flush hooks (orgops.auditing.post_flush_hook) that read uncommitted rows from the session identity map. Calling session.commit() directly bypasses these hooks because committed rows are no longer in the identity map. All persistence operations that feed the audit trail MUST use session.flush() instead of session.commit().
code:
# Flush-Before-Commit Audit Requirement

The OrgOps audit subsystem registers post-flush hooks via
`orgops.auditing.register_post_flush_hook()`. These hooks read
uncommitted (but flushed) rows from the session to generate audit
trail entries.

**CRITICAL**: If code calls `session.commit()` directly instead of
`session.flush()`, the audit hooks are BYPASSED, causing compliance
gaps in the audit trail.

## Correct Pattern
```python
# WRONG — bypasses audit hooks:
session.add_record(data)
session.commit()

# CORRECT — triggers post-flush audit hooks:
session.add_record(data)
session.flush()  # audit hooks fire here, reading uncommitted rows
```

The `orgops.auditing.post_flush_hook` sets `session._audit_triggered = True`
when it runs. If this flag is not set after persistence, the audit
subsystem raises a compliance alert.

This is a deliberate architectural choice: flush() makes rows visible
to audit hooks without ending the transaction, allowing the audit
record and the business data to be committed atomically.
